title: Gethsemane (Luke 22:39–46)
hookLine: in a garden at night he prays, sweating, not my will but yours

lines: THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DREADED THING.
cards: The night before surgery. The night before a hard goodbye. Lying awake, bargaining with the ceiling.

Across the brook Cedron from Jerusalem rises the Mount of Olives, and late this night Jesus goes there, Luke says, as he often did, and his disciples follow. Matthew and Mark name the place: Gethsemane.
John calls it a garden. Tradition says the name means oil press, where olives are crushed. Tonight he's the one being pressed.

teach.b: He tells his friends to pray that they don't fall into testing.

Then he goes a stone's throw away, kneels, and prays, in the King James Bible: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Notice what he asks first: take it away.

He doesn't pretend he wants to suffer; he asks, honestly, for another way. In Isaiah and Jeremiah, a cup can stand for suffering and judgment. Only then: nevertheless, the word Simon said over his empty nets.
Not my will, but yours. In Mark he calls God Abba, the family word for father.
Then Luke gives a detail: "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground."
As it were: Luke may mean his sweat fell heavy as blood, or that it was mixed with blood; readers have taken it both ways.
And a small honesty: some readers point out that these verses, with the angel who comes to strengthen him, are not in every early copy of Luke.
Agony is Luke's Greek word, agonia, also used for the strain of a contest, a wrestler's or a runner's. And his friends?
He comes back and finds them asleep, Luke says, sleeping for sorrow, and wakes them with a question: "Why sleep ye? rise and pray, lest ye enter into temptation."

teach.h: NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE, BE DONE.
teach.b: The shape of the prayer is plain: say what you want, all of it, and then, nevertheless.

how: Many churches keep a watch on the night of Maundy Thursday, staying up to pray in memory of Gethsemane, and some Christians keep a holy hour of prayer on other nights. Pilgrims to Jerusalem visit an olive garden on the Mount of Olives with very old trees.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Luke says plainly that he sweated blood
Luke says his sweat was as it were great drops of blood. readers take it more than one way.
Jesus first asked for the cup to be taken away
father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me. then: nevertheless.
Luke says the Mount of Olives. Matthew and Mark name Gethsemane.

games.q: you're kneeling in the garden, and you know what's coming tomorrow. what do you pray?
o: take this away from me. nevertheless, not my will.
games.why: he asks honestly for the cup to be removed, then says: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.

practice: Bring to mind the hardest thing in front of you, something you'd take away if you could, and silently say what you really want, all of it, without dressing it up: take it away, make it different, let me off.
Then, if you can, notice what it would be like to hold it a little more loosely; you don't have to get to nevertheless today. If you pray, you can pray it to God just as honestly.

orig.note: Greek: agony, the strain of a wrestler or runner in the contest. Luke's word for Jesus in the garden.
